group_assessment.weighting: Narrative review of neonatal hypoglycaemia thresholds and outcomes (no methods for study selection stated, no data). Its value here is as a class-level statement of what is recorded about glucose thresholds, dextrose gel and intravenous dextrose dosing and later neurodevelopment in otherwise healthy or at-risk newborns; it says nothing about encephalopathic infants on a deliberate low-calorie regimen, and nothing about WWOX.

entries.proposition: The article is a narrative review with no original data, and a correction for a dosage error on page 5 was issued; the text read here is the revised online version as served on the acquisition date.
entries.snippet: The original online version of this article was revised due to a dosage error identified on page 5.

entries.proposition: No datasets were generated or analysed.
entries.snippet: No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study.

entries.proposition: The review says no consensus exists among ten guidelines on the glucose value at which to intervene.
entries.snippet: No consensus existed among these guidelines regarding the specific blood glucose concentration at which intervention should be initiated or the target range at which glucose concentrations should be maintained [7].

entries.proposition: Dosing as stated: intravenous bolus 200 mg/kg (2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose) followed by 6-8 mg/kg per minute; an infusion rate above 8-10 mg/kg per minute suggests hyperinsulinism.
entries.snippet: followed by a continuous glucose infusion at a rate of 6 to 8 mg/kg per minute. A glucose infusion rate above 8–10 mg/kg/min strongly suggests the diagnosis of hyperinsulinism

entries.proposition: Figure 3 heads the escalation step as glucose infusion above 10-12 mg/kg/hr, a different unit and range from the 8-10 mg/kg per minute in the text.
entries.snippet: Visual attestation of Figure 3: three-step treatment flow; third header reads 'Glucose infusion > 10-12 mg/kg/hr'; second step 'Glucose infusion (200 mg/kg bolus plus 6 to 8 mg/kg/min)'; first step buccal glucose gel 40% at 200-400 mg per kg.

experimental_context.system: narrative synthesis figure, neonatal hypoglycaemia treatment

entries.proposition: The glucose gel dose is 200-400 mg/kg of a 40% gel, recommended for initial hypoglycaemia unresponsive to feeding.
entries.snippet: It should be administered at 200–400 mg per kg and is recommended for initial or transitional hypoglycemia unresponsive to early feeding.

entries.proposition: The review cites rodent evidence that glucose infusion worsened neuronal death in insulin-induced hypoglycaemia through superoxide, a reason for controlled rather than uncontrolled glucose delivery.
entries.snippet: Experimental studies in rodents have shown that glucose infusion worsens neuronal death in insulin-induced hypoglycemia by increasing superoxide production, suggestive of therapeutic administration of uncontrolled glucose delivery proving to be detrimental by worsening the initial neuronal injury [18].

entries.proposition: The review states that lactate or ketones do not fully replace glucose in meeting neuronal demand.
entries.snippet: Supplementation with lactate or ketones does not entirely meet the cellular demand that glucose is able to provide.

entries.proposition: Diazoxide with chlorothiazide is routinely combined to prevent fluid overload, and one low-dose RCT found no fluid overload.
entries.snippet: In current practice, chlorothiazide and diazoxide are routinely used together to prevent fluid overload.

entries.proposition: The non-inferiority trial that supports a 36 mg/dL threshold excluded infants whose first glucose was below 36 mg/dL and enrolled only 'healthy' infants.
entries.snippet: By study design, newborn infants with initial blood glucose concentrations < 36 mg/dL (2 mol/L) were excluded from this study [9].

entries.proposition: Follow-up cohorts link severe or recurrent neonatal hypoglycaemia (below about 36 mg/dL) to later executive and visual-motor deficits at 4.5 years, and below 30 mg/dL to lower IQ at 7-11 years; at 2 years no impairment was seen.
entries.snippet: However, children with severe hypoglycemia (< 36 mg/dL or 2 mmol/L), recurrent hypoglycemia, or clinically undetected hypoglycemia (detected only through continuous glucose monitoring) exhibited lower scores in executive and visual-motor functions.

entries.proposition: In the Roeper cohort two or more episodes below 30 mg/dL were not associated with worse outcomes, which sits beside the summary claim that a single severe episode may cause adverse outcomes.
entries.snippet: Two or more episodes of blood glucose less than 30 mg/dL (1.7 mmol/L) were not associated with significantly worse outcomes.

entries.proposition: The Summary gives 47 mg/dL in the first 48 h and 60 mg/dL after as safe thresholds, in the same paragraph as an advice to keep values above 36 mg/dL.
entries.snippet: Blood glucose > 47 mg/dL (2.6 mmol/L) in the first 48 h of life and > 60 mg/dL (3.3 mmol/L) after 48 h are not associated with adverse neurological outcomes and may be used as safe thresholds.

entries.proposition: The text puts the day-4 plasma plateau at 89 +/- 13 mg/dL while Figure 2A plots 82-83 mg/dL for 72-120 h.
entries.snippet: a final steady-state concentration plateau of 89 + / − 13 mg/dL (4.9 + / − 0.7 mmol/L) was reached by the fourth day of life.

entries.proposition: Figure 2A shows plasma glucose means of 57, 57, 59, 60, 69, 82 and 83 mg/dL across the age bands and interstitial values at or slightly below them in the first 24 h.
entries.snippet: Visual attestation of Figure 2A: plasma glucose (mean + SD) 57, 57, 59, 60, 69, 82, 83 mg/dL for 0-4, 4-12, 12-24, 24-48, 48-72, 72-96, 96-120 h; interstitial row 54, 55, 59, 59, 69, 82, 83; panel B 10th percentile 47 mg/dL below 48 h and 54 above 72 h.
